A close reading for the week

“Afraid! Of Him?”

The Wind in the Willows · Chapter VII

In the middle of a book about a boastful toad and a cosy riverbank, two small animals meet a god face to face. It may be the strangest, most rapturous chapter in English children’s literature, and it ends by taking the memory away.

… he looked in the very eyes of the Friend and Helper; saw the backward sweep of the curved horns, gleaming in the growing daylight; saw the stern, hooked nose between the kindly eyes1 that were looking down on them humorously, while the bearded mouth broke into a half-smile at the corners; … saw, last of all, nestling between his very hooves, sleeping soundly… the little, round, podgy, childish form of the baby otter.2

  1. 1

    The god is terrible and kind

    Grahame’s Pan has “curved horns” and a “stern, hooked nose”, the ancient, faintly frightening face of the goat-god, set between “kindly eyes” that look down “humorously”. Every fearsome feature is paired with a gentle one. The divine is awe-inspiring and loving in the same face, and the animals cannot separate the two: dread and comfort arrive together.

  2. 2

    The god as protector

    The vision resolves, “last of all”, on the lost baby otter safe “between his very hooves”. The whole apparition of the pagan god exists, in the story, to return a lost child. Grahame brings the divine down to a riverbank, where Pan is doing the tender work of keeping a baby otter safe until morning. Cosmic awe is placed at the service of ordinary rescue.
